The Game Developing Fish

When a fish is bored it just keeps on swimming, but when Fish is bored he makes games. With all this ocean for inspiration, he has a lot of ideas, and he wants to make them all. He is a passionate gamer and game developer with strong expertise in C# and the Unity engine, and solid skills in C++ and Unreal Engine 4/5. He has a few well recieved games under his belt (which he leaves at home cause he's a fish, and fish don't wear belts) that he made with the help of ocean-dewlling friends he's met along the way.
Using his tools he peers into the depths of the ocean and brings his ideas to life. He loves to experiment with other fish tools that he picks up along the way, but he is also intrigued by strange tools for different species like crabs, octopuses and even birds. He finds ways of using them to upgrade his own tools, learn, grow, and come closer to his ultimate goal:
To Become the World's Greatest Game Developing Fish!

Assassin's Creed – Black Flag Resynced Ubisoft Belgrade

AAA production at Ubisoft Belgrade, in C++ and Ubisoft's in-house Anvil Engine, focusing mainly on UI development. Assassin's Creed – Black Flag Resynced revisits the pirate adventure of Edward Kenway, combining open-world exploration, naval combat, stealth, and melee combat in a Caribbean setting during the Golden Age of Piracy. The remaster shows a great leap in visual fidelity, with enhanced graphics, improved character models, and more detailed environments. The team worked hard to refine the gameplay in its entirety, ensuring a fantastic experience that honors the original while introducing new features and improvements. The release results speak for themselves: the game has been well received by both critics and players, with praise for its stunning visuals, engaging gameplay, and faithful representation of the original story. The project was a testament to the dedication and skill of the development team, who worked tirelessly to deliver a polished and immersive experience for fans of the franchise.

Apocalypse Express Llamaware

Apocalypse Express is an indie action-management roguelite set in a post-apocalyptic wasteland, where survival depends on keeping a heavily armed train operational against relentless waves of enemies. Players must balance combat, resource collection, repairs, and fuel management while upgrading train modules to create increasingly powerful and specialized builds. With a wide range of weapons, defensive systems, upgrades, and relics, each run offers opportunities to experiment with different strategies and adapt to escalating threats. The game combines fast-paced combat with demanding real-time decision-making, challenging players to manage chaos and push their train as far as possible through the remains of the old world.
I worked as a game developer in a small team with a big dream. It was an amazing journey and I had a blast working on the game with the team. I got hands-on experience with many different parts of the game. The development process was open to the community, and its feedback helped us polish the game into what it is today. The reviews have been overwhelmingly positive, which is, if I may say, very impressive for a debut project. It's a joyride to play and work on, and I'm incredibly happy and proud to have been a part of it.

Infernal Dante

Overview

Infernal Dante is my ongoing Unreal project. The gameplay is written in C++, with Blueprint on top for the parts that are faster to iterate on by hand.

The project is a roguelite exploration/fighting game following a small Italian greyhound protagonist, with a focus on exploration, movement and combat. The player will explore a (hopefully) procedurally generated world, fighting enemies and collecting loot to improve their character.

For this project I'm tackling many problems at once: narrative, modeling, rigging, animation, input, movement, abilities, music and sound design, and the flow between them in order to get a better feel for the entire development pipeline and the various disciplines involved in making a game. Each of these areas is a learning experience, and the project is a sandbox for me to explore them in a way that lets me see the results immediately.

The project is still in its very early stages, and I'm currently focusing on getting the movement and combat systems working together. Once I have a solid foundation, I'll be able to iterate on the gameplay and narrative, and add more content to the game.

What I'm working on

  • Satisfying and fun character movement, with terrain interaction providing a responsive feel
  • Setting up the Gameplay Ability System and the flow between abilities and stats
  • Hitbox-based combat with action camera
  • Animation montages with notify-driven traces for hit detection
  • Enhanced Input mappings for every player action handled in C++
  • Setting up the model, rig and animation pipeline between Blender and Unreal
  • Hands-on experience with the entire game development pipeline, from concept to playable prototype

Technologies

  • Unreal Engine 5.5.4
  • C++
  • Visual Studio
  • Blueprint
  • Gameplay Ability System
  • Enhanced Input
  • Blender

Features

  • Modeling

    First and foremost, we need a protagonist. I got into Blender, watched a few tutorials, and came up with this little guy. Isn't he adorable...

  • Movement and Animation

    For the very start of the project I focused on getting the main character moving, as this would help me get a feel for the movement mechanics. It's important to have the movement feel deliberate and stick to the theme of a little speedy demon. I also wanted to get a feel for the workflow between Blender and Unreal, so I could iterate on the character's movement and animations quickly.
    Initially I created animations for idle, walking, running, sprinting, and jumping vertically and horizontally. Both the movement and jumping animations were then used to make 1D Blend Spaces in UE5, and the Blend Spaces were used to blend between these animations based on the character's speed.

  • Fun movement

    I'm currently working on making the movement feel better by introducing inertia, obstacles, and adaptive foot placement. It's still in its very early stages, so there's nothing to show yet.

Gallery

  • 3D Model

    A rough model of a teacup Italian Greyhound. A Tiggy™, if you will. (And yes, they exist). It's deffinetly not perfect and the paint job is kinda rough, but considering this was my first ever modeling project and I wanted to do it as quickly as possible, I'm happy with how it turned out. The proportions may look a little out of whack, but it's just a very small dog. In reality, the head and eyes are only slightly exaggerated for maximum cuteness.

Combat Demo

Overview

A small, self-contained combat sandbox. The aim was to make a playable prototype that would let me explore the interaction between animations and the Gameplay Ability System, and to get a feel for how to structure combat code in Unreal Engine.

While working on this project I created some attack abilities, a dash ability, and a few enemy behaviors. I also set up a basic camera system, and a simple UI to display the player's health and stamina.

The most interesting part for me was figuring out the combo system, which allowed chaining animations to keep the combat feeling fluid. This allowed for randomized attack patterns and a more dynamic combat experience. I also learned a lot about how to structure the code for abilities and how to use the Gameplay Ability System effectively.

The project is just a proof of concept that was limited to free assets, so it lacks polish and content, but it was a great learning experience.

What I'm working on

  • One feature I implemented myself, start to finish: a combo system for a fighting game that features chaining animations
  • Randomized player attack animations for variety
  • Driving the Gameplay Ability System with animation notifies to handle hit detection and ability activation
  • Using Gameplay Attributes to manage player stats and effects, and interact with the ability system

Technologies

  • Unreal Engine
  • C++
  • Visual Studio
  • GAS
  • Animation Montages
  • Notify-driven hit detection

Features

  • Punch Combo

    The full combo consists of 4 punches. When the player presses the Punch button, animations from 4 pools are selected randomly at the start. While the player is holding the Punch button, the character performs the combo. Releasing the button will interrupt the combo.
    It is implemented as a Gameplay Ability to streamline its interaction with other abilities and stamina.

  • Kick Combo

    The full combo consists of 4 kicks. When the player presses the Kick button, animations from 4 pools are selected randomly at the start. While the player is holding the Kick button, the character performs the combo. Releasing the button will interrupt the combo.
    Just like the punch, the kick is a Gameplay Ability.

  • Slam Ability

    This ability plays a slam animation, and does AOE damage to surrounding enemies and knocks them back. Triggering this ability will interrupt basic attacks.

  • Dash Ability

    The dash ability is implemented as a Gameplay Ability, and is driven by an animation. When triggered it interrupts all combat abilities, and the dash ability can be used to dodge attacks or close the distance to enemies.

  • Chaining Combos

    As all the combat and movement abilities are Gameplay Abilities, they can seamlessly integrate with GAS. By leveraging this I was able to implement a simple animation chaining setup, and used Gameplay Tags to manage animation interruptions using the hierarchy Dash > Slam > Attack.

  • Enemy Behavior

    The enemy behavior is implemented as a simple state machine. The enemy patrols. When it sees the player (I know it has no eyes), it attacks in melee if the player is in range, and otherwise aims and shoots at them.

Shooter Demo

Overview

Created as a project to explore third-person shooting mechanics, ECS, and combining animations for omnidirectional running and shooting. There are some unique challenges to making a third-person shooter feel realistic and good, and it was very interesting to tackle these issues. For instance, the walking animation should have good ground traction in all directions, and the projectile trajectory should look realistic for both hip fire and ADS. It was fun to do the projectile calculations; I felt like a NASA scientist for a bit.
By the end I even picked up materials for a bit and made a neat circular crosshair... a circle hair... Anyway, it ended up working really well, and I'm happy with it and its potential.

What I'm working on

  • Ballistic projectiles that are shot from the weapon towards the point where the crosshair is aiming
  • Blending animations for the legs (walking) and torso (shooting)
  • ADS system that modifies the camera angle and shooting accuracy
  • Modular design using ECS allowing for faster production of different similar entities

Technologies

  • Unreal Engine 5
  • C++
  • Visual Studio
  • Materials

Features

  • Ballistics

    I wanted the projectiles to be ballistic, and I wanted to see them flying from the gun to where I was aiming. For this I had to calculate the bullet's trajectory from the start point (gun muzzle) to the target point (line trace from the crosshair). Once the trajectory was calculated it was a simple matter of instantiating the bullet with these parameters, and letting it fly.

  • ADS

    Since this is a third-person shooter, the ADS camera doesn't become an FPS camera. Instead, it comes over the character's shoulder and reduces the FOV. This has a smooth animation and triggers UI elements to update. Aiming down sights is very accurate, and hip fire introduces randomness to the trajectory.

  • Animation Blending

    I wanted the legs to run, and the torso to aim and shoot, but I had separate animations for each. By using animation blueprints I was able to blend these two animations and use both on the same model, where the shooting animation controls the torso and the walking animation controls the legs. By using 2D blendspaces for the leg animation, I was able to support omnidirectional animated walking and crouching.
    Unfortunately the free animation pack I was using only had 4 cardinal directions of movement, so the forward-left blend ended up looking a little weird, but the other directions worked great.
    Also I dipped into programmatically controlling the animation, adding another layer of blending. This was done to curve the spine as the player looks up and down, so he always faces screen forward.

  • Custom UI

    Created a simple lightweight crosshair widget to help with aiming and give more visual feedback on the accuracy. I went with the circle design because I've always preferred that style, and it does a better job of representing where your bullets might land.
    This crosshair doesn't have a source image, only a material; it is procedurally rendered, so modifying its material, radius, feather, color, and opacity can be done on the fly, and tweaking a little more can even produce some interesting shapes. Further, the resizing is controlled by the player's ADS animation and the maximum radius is determined by the character's accuracy stat, so the player state, camera and UI are perfectly in sync.

  • ECS

    As I was finishing the character, I realized that I could potentially develop this game further in the future and add more character variety. For this it would be practical to modularize some elements, so I decided to extract the aiming and shooting functionality into some entity components. Now each character only needs to add these components, plug in all the wires, and it has all the gear it needs ready to go. Nice!

  • Enemy Towers

    Finally I wanted to make a tower with a gun to have fun with targeting. When the tower has no target it just swivels randomly in a 'search' pattern. As soon as a character enters the tower's range, it gets tracked and shot at. Running around helps dodge the bullets once you're at a certain distance, but your best bet is just to shoot it down.

Shaders in Unity

Overview

I wanted to dip my toes into shaders, some online tutorials led me to try out Unity's URP for making shaders, and in the end I wrote my own shaders in HLSL because I didn't like doing things in the graph, but the end results look pretty much the same. The animations were a different story though, and I would never even attempt this in any graph, but never say never... who knows...
Anyway, the project ended up being very fun and instructive, and I got to make some beautiful mathematical shapes to tickle your brain :)
Note: I'm using the term 'wave function' here a lot to talk about sine waves and more complex wave functions, nothing to do with quantum mechanics in case any quantum physicists are reading.

What I'm working on

  • Make a material for a heat map
  • Make cool shapes

Technologies

  • Unity Engine
  • C#
  • Shader Graph
  • HLSL

Features

  • Making the Material

    To have a good visualization of how the points are moving, I wanted to introduce a material that changes color based on its position. This was fairly simple and can be done in a shader graph or HLSL.
    Putting the material on a cube allows us to see this effect happen in real time.

  • Simple Sine

    Okay, the color itself isn't that interesting. I started experimenting with placing the cubes, now tiny to represent points, in a line and moving them using a simple sine wave.
    By tweaking the sine function we can manipulate the shape of the resulting curve to get interesting effects.

  • Complex Sine

    We can also extend this to the 3rd dimension by making a plane of points and manipulating them with perpendicular wave functions. Complex wave functions produce some interesting shapes.

  • Surfaces

    The surface manipulation is especially hypnotic to me for some reason. I love watching the simulation run. More complex functions are used here, and different wave functions can even be overlapped.

  • Going 3D

    If you thought the last one was hypnotic, this is gonna blow you away. By doing some shader magic I was able to make some amazing 3D geometry animations.

  • More 3D

    Finally, everyone's favorite shape - the Torus! I added some random noise at the end for an interesting effect. What else is there to say, enjoy the visuals.
